questions.subject: HUMAN_GEOGRAPHY
questions.topic: What counts as an urban place
questions.learningObjective: Define what counts as an urban place
questions.stem: Item 0001: a settlement has high density and built-up land; does it count as urban?

options.text: An urban place is defined by population density and built-up land.
Any settlement with a mayor counts as urban.
Only national capitals are urban.
Rural villages with farms are urban.

questions.explanation: Urban status usually depends on density and built-up land, not on governance, capital status, or rural functions. A village with farms remains rural.

provenance.author: bank-team-human-geography
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: HUMAN_GEOGRAPHY
questions.topic: Urban area and metropolitan area
questions.learningObjective: Distinguish urban area from metropolitan area
questions.stem: Item 0002: a map shows contiguous built-up land and a wider commuting zone; which is the metropolitan area?

options.text: They are always the same boundary.
Urban area is contiguous built-up land; metropolitan area includes commuting ties.
Metropolitan area excludes suburbs.
Urban area includes all commuting zones.

questions.explanation: The urban area covers contiguous built-up land, while the metropolitan area adds commuting and economic ties. They are not automatically the same.

provenance.author: bank-team-human-geography
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: HUMAN_GEOGRAPHY
questions.topic: Boundary and footprint on a municipal map
questions.learningObjective: Distinguish boundary from footprint on a map
questions.stem: Item 0003: a municipal map shows a city boundary and a built-up footprint; how do they differ?

answer.exemplar: The boundary marks legal jurisdiction, while the footprint shows the actual built-up land, so a city can have a large legal area with a smaller physical footprint.

questions.explanation: Legal boundaries and physical footprints often differ. The boundary sets jurisdiction, while the footprint shows where development actually occurs.

provenance.author: bank-team-human-geography
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: HUMAN_GEOGRAPHY
questions.topic: Primate city and the primacy it implies
questions.learningObjective: Explain what a primate city is
questions.stem: Item 0004: the largest city has 4 million people and the second has 1 million; compute the primacy ratio.
questions.explanation: Divide 4 million by 1 million to get 4. A ratio this large suggests strong primate-city dominance.

provenance.author: bank-team-human-geography
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: HUMAN_GEOGRAPHY
questions.topic: Average annual urban growth rate
questions.learningObjective: Explain average annual urban growth rate

stimulus.body: A clinician's note records an urban population rising from 100000 to 160000 over 5 years. The note asks for the average annual growth rate.

questions.stem: Item 0005: which formula is correct?

options.text: It ignores starting population.
options.misconception: omits base population in growth rate

options.text: It is simple division of total growth by years.
options.misconception: uses simple instead of compound growth

options.text: It is the compound annual rate that links initial and final populations.
It is always the same as birth rate.
options.misconception: confuses urban growth with natural increase

questions.explanation: Average annual growth uses compound growth between the initial and final populations. Simple division or birth rate alone would misstate the rate.
questions.hint: Use compound growth over the period.

provenance.author: bank-team-human-geography
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: HUMAN_GEOGRAPHY
questions.topic: Testing a rank-size pattern against a table
questions.learningObjective: Test a rank-size pattern against a table
questions.stem: Item 0006: a table lists city populations by rank; what does rank-size predict?

options.text: It predicts random population order.
It predicts equal population for all ranks.
It predicts growth only for top cities.
Rank-size predicts population proportional to 1/rank.

questions.explanation: Rank-size predicts population inversely proportional to rank. Equal sizes, top-only growth, or randomness are not the rule.

provenance.author: bank-team-human-geography
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: HUMAN_GEOGRAPHY
questions.topic: Rank-size index at a single rank
questions.learningObjective: Explain a rank-size index at one rank
questions.stem: Item 0007: at rank 3, actual population is 320000 and predicted is 333333; what does the index show?

options.text: It measures only total city count.
The index compares actual population to the rank-size prediction.
It is the city's rank alone.
It measures land area of the city.

questions.explanation: The rank-size index compares actual population with the value predicted by the rank-size rule. Rank alone, city count, or land area do not measure fit.

provenance.author: bank-team-human-geography
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: HUMAN_GEOGRAPHY
questions.topic: What the rank-size rule assumes
questions.learningObjective: Explain what the rank-size rule assumes
questions.stem: Item 0008: a rank-size rule is applied to a city system; what does it assume?

options.text: It assumes only one primate city exists.
It assumes all cities are the same size.
It assumes a regular hierarchy with constant scaling across ranks.
It assumes no migration occurs.
options.misconception: adds migration assumption not in rule

questions.explanation: Rank-size assumes a regular hierarchical system with consistent scaling between ranks. Equal sizes, primacy, or migration are not its core assumption.

provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used
